title: The Almost Locker
premise: Theo Thornbury has survived high school in the tiny town of Marrow Creek by being careful: out, but quiet; present, but invisible. When their English teacher assigns a college essay answering 'What is the truest thing about you?' anonymously, the essays get read aloud, and one of them—raw, furious, and unmistakably Theo's—ignites a firestorm that exposes secrets across the whole senior class. As suspicion narrows and friendships fracture, Theo must choose between protecting the people who once protected them and claiming a truth that could cost them everything. In the end, Theo claims the essay publicly at graduation, discovering that belonging was never something they had to earn—it was something they had to stop hiding from.
about_author: Dominic Okafor is a former small-town debate coach who writes stories about kids who talk back to silence. He lives in Ohio with his partner and an ill-tempered cat named Verdict.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Ways to Be Careful
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. We meet Marrow Creek through Theo's meticulous survival routines: which hallways, which jokes, which silences. A small moment—a hand brushed in the library with closeted classmate Wes—shows what Theo wants but won't reach for. Emotional beat: weary resignation sharpened by longing.

chapters.title: The Prompt
chapters.summary: Ms. Alvarez assigns the anonymous essay: 'What is the truest thing about you?' Theo's POV. At home, Theo writes three drafts and burns two, finally typing something honest at 2 a.m. and submitting it half-hoping it disappears into the pile. Beat: reckless hope disguised as surrender.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Alvarez reads selected essays anonymously; Theo's lands like a detonation—the room goes electric, and popular girl Priya's essay admits she faked her way into belonging too. Theo's POV, watching classmates guess. Beat: terror and a strange, intoxicating freedom.

chapters.title: The Hunt
chapters.summary: Wes's POV. The school turns detective; Wes, terrified his own secret sits adjacent to Theo's, joins the guessing game to deflect suspicion. He watches Theo lie smoothly and feels both grateful and sick. Beat: complicity as self-protection, loyalty curdling.

chapters.title: Priya Knows
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Priya deduces the truth via a repeated phrase from Theo's essay and confronts them—not to expose them, but to bargain: her father runs the school board, and she needs an ally against him. Beat: uneasy alliance between two kinds of invisibility.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A photo of the essay circulates on a burner account; the town's Facebook groups ignite. Theo's mother, who suspected but never asked, finally does—and Theo can't answer. Beat: the private becoming public, family fault lines cracking open.

chapters.title: What Wes Did
chapters.summary: Wes's POV. Cornered by teammates, Wes names Theo to save himself. The betrayal isn't dramatic—it's quiet, a shrug in a locker room—and that's what breaks Theo. Beat: devastating loss of first love and faith in loyalty.

chapters.title: The Board Meeting
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The school board moves to punish the essay's author and censure Alvarez; Priya publicly breaks with her father, revealing the leak traced to student records he accessed. Chaos erupts, but Theo stays silent while others fight for them. Beat: shame at being defended without standing up.

chapters.title: Graduation Day
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the ceremony, before diplomas are handed out, Theo walks to the mic during the student address slot Wes surrendered and reads the essay aloud, unedited, naming themselves. Silence, then Priya stands, then half the gym. Beat: cathartic climax—truth chosen over safety.

chapters.title: The Truest Thing
chapters.summary: Weeks later, packing for college. Wes shows up uninvited to apologize; Theo doesn't forgive him fully, but lets him help carry boxes—an honest, incomplete ending. Ms. Alvarez's letter reveals she knew all along and submitted Theo's essay to a magazine. Beat: earned, imperfect belonging; leaving home already free.
